Govt approves ‘extraordinary security allowance’ for police, civil service officers in 26 KP districts. PESHAWAR: The federal government has designated 26 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) as “terror-affected”, declaring that all Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS) and Police Service of Pakistan (PSP) officers posted therein are eligible for an ‘extraordinary law and order and security risk allowance’, effective from July 1 this year, it emerged on Saturday. According to a notification issued by the Establishment Division to the KP chief secretary and seen by Dawn , the allowance for 26 of the 35 districts will be 250 per cent of the running basic pay and paid retroactively. It read that the ‘KP Extraordinary Law, Order and Security Risk Allowance’ would be admissible to PAS and PSP officers posted in Peshawar, Khyber, Mardan, Charsadda, Nowshera, Mohmand, Kohat, Hangu, Karak, Kurram, Orakzai, Bannu, Lakki Marwat, North Waziristan, Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Upper and Lower South Waziristan, Swat, Buner, Shangla, Bajaur, Upper and Lower Dir, besides Upper and Lower Chitral. Citing an August 18 letter from the Establishment Division to the KP chief secretary, the notification stated that Swabi and the entirety of Hazara Division, comprising Abbottabad, Haripur, Mansehra, Battagram, Torghar, Kolai-Palas and the Upper and Lower Kohistan districts, were “excluded for the purpose of admissibility of subject allowance”. The federal government requested the KP government to proceed with payment of the allowance with effect from July 1, 2026. In the August letter seen by Dawn , the Establishment Division said the government approved the grant for PAS and PSP officers serving in the “seriously disturbed KP districts”, due to the law and order situation and the danger to officers and personnel. It added that the allowance would be admissible only to PAS and PSP officers in districts categorised as seriously disturbed, which would be identified by the Interior and Narcotics Control Division at the start of each financial year. “Establishment Division will notify the districts where this allowance will be admissible, on [an] annual basis, at the start of each financial year,” the letter read. “The allowance shall be discontinued upon transfer of the officers from the notified districts.” It further stated that the allowance would be provided during sanctioned leave of any kind, except extraordinary leave, and would not be available during suspension, appointment as an officer on special duty, or training of any kind. Furthermore, it would not be treated as part of emoluments for the purpose of calculating pension and gratuity, and the cost of the allowance would be borne by the federal government. KP has seen a rise in terrorist attacks over the past year. According to the Annual Security Report 2025 from the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), KP recorded a significant surge in violence last year as “fatalities rose from 1,620 in 2024 to 2,331 in 2025”. Due to a resurgence of terrorism, especially in KP and Balochistan, where attacks often target security personnel and LEAs , the state has intensified counter-terrorism operations. According to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), mainland KP recorded 54 terrorist attacks last month, marking a 50 per cent increase compared to July. Meanwhile, the merged districts recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August, marking a 126pc increase.

Trump says Houthis have asked US not to intervene in Yemen. United States President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthi fighters, who have seized a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia, have asked Washington not to intervene. The Houthis have taken control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast after capturing three strategic islands in a lightning offensive. Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has relied on the area ever since Iran’s Hormuz blockade choked off its shipments via the Gulf. “The Houthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump told reporters on a visit to Dublin, Ireland. “They don’t want us to go after them.” He added that “everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy,” in the region. Trump also mentioned having spoken to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom he described as a “friend”. According to US outlet Axios , the Saudi crown prince called Trump twice on Thursday to request US strikes on the Houthis, but the American president declined. The Houthis also targeted Saudi Arabian oil facilities this week with a massive drone and missile attack. Yemeni govt forces hit Houthis in Mocha In Yemen, the government forces said on Saturday they have struck Houthi fighters in the strategic Red Sea city of Mocha. Men gesture in a screen grab from a video released on Sept 11, 2026 and said to show Khaled bin Walid camp after Houthis captured the city of Mocha in Taiz Province. — Al-Masirah TV/Handout via Reuters Following a week-long offensive, the Houthis on Friday captured Yemen’s Red Sea coast, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait , a vital artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the US-Iran war. “The armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime,” near the port of the city of Mocha, the government news agency Saba reported. The spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they have also struck the Houthis’ “vehicles and members” on the Mocha-Dhubab road, 11 kilometres from the city, according to Saba . Nazili said on Friday they had begun shelling areas in Mocha, and called on citizens not to use the Taiz-Mocha and Mocha-Dhubab roads. The Houthis seized control of Mocha on Thursday, with their attack driving many to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based. On Friday, Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha’s airport , while a local official said the city’s seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin. The Houthi offensive, which started last week , has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides. It has also displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday. It is part of renewed hostilities in Yemen’s civil war that began with the group’s takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.

CM Bugti says 'no dialogue' with those taking up arms against state. Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti said on Saturday there would be “no dialogue in any case” with those who took up arms against the state. He made the remarks while speaking via video link to the country’s media anchors, senior journalists and other representatives at the Chief Minister’s Secretariat on Saturday, according to a statement issued by his office. CM Bugti said the war against terrorism would continue in Balochistan until the “last terrorist” was eliminated, adding that it was not possible to control the entire province while sitting in Quetta. He affirmed that the civil and military leadership were united against terrorism and there was “no ambiguity or confusion” on the matter. The chief minister noted that security forces were performing their duties in difficult circumstances in Balochistan, adding that state institutions were working in complete coordination in the fight against terrorism. Before the talk with journalists, CM Bugti was also provided multiple briefings covering the provincial government’s strategy for social and economic development, governance and service delivery, effective use of development funds, and measures to ensure that development projects benefited the people. A briefing on minerals and mining highlighted the sector’s potential, ongoing projects and measures being taken to develop it and better utilise the province’s mineral resources, the statement said. The Ministry of Interior and Tribal Affairs also briefed the chief minister on the law and order situation, the Provincial Action Plan, police reforms and progress on the integration of the Levies Force into the police, the statement added. Bugti was also briefed on the Safe City project, legislation and coordination among law-enforcement agencies. During the interaction with journalists, CM Bugti also expressed his views on the creation of new administrative units, saying, “If new provinces are to be created in Balochistan, they should be on administrative rather than linguistic grounds.” On Thursday, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said the Parliament was expected to debate the issue of new provinces next month. Speaking to mediapersons, Bugti said he had no knowledge of any “ two-and-a-half-year government agreement ” for Balochistan, according to the statement. The decision to change the government had to be taken by the political leadership, he said, adding that his cabinet would continue to serve the people as long as they were in office. The chief minister was quoted as saying that although he could not claim that corruption across the province had been completely eliminated, it had decreased compared to the past. Measures were being taken to ensure merit in all government departments, including educational institutions, he added. He said development projects in Balochistan had been completed in record time compared to the past, adding that the provincial government was focused on making the development process effective, result-oriented and aligned with public needs. Referring to the return of foreign nationals, Bugti said that 1.1 million Afghan refugees, along with other foreigners, had been sent back to their homeland from Balochistan. On the issue of missing persons, he said the matter was sometimes presented on national media and other forums without proper context, which did not reflect the true picture of the situation. “Terrorism was not an issue of one province but of the entire country and required joint efforts at the national level for its elimination”, Bugti was quoted as saying.

ECP promotes four officers to BS-20, transfers 54 across country amid reshuffle. ISLAMABAD: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) has announced a major administrative reshuffle, promoting four BS-19 officers to BS-20 and transferring 54 BS-17 officials across the country with immediate effect. The orders, issued with the approval of the Chief Election Commissioner, also include key postings at the provincial and secretariat levels. According to a notification, four officers have been promoted from BS-19 to BS-20 on a regular basis and placed on one-year probation. The promoted officers include Fazal Hakeem and Abdul Lag. Hakeem, the Regional Election Commissioner in Peshawar, has been posted as Additional Director General (Elections-II) at the ECP Secretariat in Islamabad. Lag, Director (Elections) at ECP Balochistan, will serve as Joint Provincial Election Commissioner (Elections) in Balochistan. Khurshid Alam, Director to the CEC, has been posted as ADG to the CEC. The ECP has also upgraded and redesignated his previous BS-19 post. Nazar Abbas, ADG (Electoral Rolls) OPS, has been posted as ADG (Electoral Rolls) at the ECP Secretariat and promoted to BS-20. In a related notification, Syed Waseem Ahmed Jafri, Joint PEC (Elections), BS-20, has been transferred from Balochistan to Sindh. 54 BS-17 officers transferred The largest set of changes came through another notification, which ordered the transfers and postings of 54 Assistant Election Commissioners and Assistant Directors in BS-17. The transfers cover all four provinces and involve wide-scale movement between field offices and the ECP Secretariat in Islamabad. Several officers have been brought to the Secretariat to serve in key wings, including Confidential, Protocol, HRMS, Record and LGE. Among those transferred to the Secretariat are Zoya Kanwal as Assistant Director (Confidential), Ayesha Hamid as AD (LGE-KP), Adil Ahmad Shahzad as AD (Protocol), and Syeda Javeria as AD (HRMS). Field postings include Shabir Ahmed Shah, who has been moved from REC Rakhshan to DEC Kharan; Imran Khan Abbasi, from REC Shaheed Benazirabad to DEC Shikarpur; and Shahab Siddique, from DEC Bannu to PEC Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Coalition partners PPP, PML-N seek to bridge differences amid strained ties. LAHORE: Differences continued to mar the working relationship between the PPP and PML-N as the coalition partners’ coordination committees met on Saturday to resolve outstanding issues and iron out their differences. The PML-N-led government enjoys a two-thirds majority in the National Asse­mbly with the PPP’s support. The meeting, held after months of strained relations during the acrimonious election campaigns in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan , did not go smoothly, according to insiders. The PPP delegation included former prime minister Raja Pervaiz Ashraf, Punjab Governor Sardar Saleem Haider Khan, Hassan Murtaza, Qamar Zaman Kaira and Ali Qasim Gilani. Representing the PML-N were Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah and Khawaja Saad Rafique. The PPP protested that, as a coalition partner, it was paying a heavy political price for the PML-N government’s failure on multiple fronts, including runaway inflation, rising petroleum prices, the unresolved farming crisis, load-shedding and delays in local government elections. The PML-N, on the other hand, maintained that instead of acting as a coalition partner and sharing responsibility, the PPP was behaving more like an opposition party and exploiting public issues for political gains, despite knowing that the government had little control over factors such as petroleum prices and inflation. “There were moments of heated debate, but tempers soon cooled as both sides knew that they had no option but to work together as political guarantors of the system,” one of the participants told Dawn . The PML-N also invited Punjab Inspector General of Police Rao Abdul Karim to address the PPP’s concerns relating to police matters and assured the party of its share in development schemes. The PPP, however, recalled that previous decisions taken on both matters had not been implemented and had effectively been forgotten. However, the bad blood and trust deficit that had built up over months of acrimonious relations between the two coalition partners may take several more meetings and confidence-building measures to overcome, the participant said, adding: “Both sides agreed to implement decisions taken previously, meet more regularly and work together to improve governance.” The two sides also agreed to maintain the consultation process and continue working together to resolve differences and address coalition-related matters through mutual understanding and in the national interest. The PPP and PML-N were engaged in a war of words following the PML-N’s emergence as the winner of the first phase of elections in AJK. Last week, the PPP questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence over the debate on creating new provinces and sought his stance on the matter. The PPP had earlier maintained that any move to create additional federating units must follow the procedure laid down in the Constitution. However, the PPP-led Sindh government on Wednesday got a resolution passed by the provincial assembly opposing any further division of the country’s existing four provinces.

England survive scare to seal 3-0 sweep against Pakistan. Joe Root led from the front as England survived a major wobble to beat Pakistan by eight wickets in the third Test at Edgbaston on Saturday, sealing a 3-0 series whitewash. The home team, chasing just 130 to win, were in deep trouble when openers Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay were dismissed in the first over, bowled by Mohammad Abbas. Root, England’s record run-scorer, edged his first ball, bowled by Razaullah, through the slips for four in a nervy start but settled and scored quickly to take the sting out of the situation. The captain was given a huge reprieve when he chopped onto the stumps off Mohammad Ali, only for the umpire to signal a no ball, leaving the bowler distraught. Root, with Jordan Cox at the other end, had another let-off when he edged an Abbas delivery between first and second slip, with neither fielder moving. But he reached his half-century off 57 balls with a cut for four and Cox reached the landmark shortly afterwards. England reached their target in the 25th over, with Root unbeaten on 62 and Cox 59 not out. Root, in his second spell as England skipper after the departure of Ben Stokes, admitted his team were not the finished article but said he was delighted with their series win. “The amount of uncertainty, noise and I guess chaos there was coming into the series, the way the guys have dealt with that – being so clinical with what we’ve had in front of us – and be stood here with a 3-0 win is really pleasing,” he told Sky Sports. “It sets us up nicely looking ahead to the start of a new era with (new head coach) Stephen Fleming coming in.” Pakistan woes England celebrated their first Test series win since 2024 while Pakistan have now lost 16 of their past 21 games and are rooted at the bottom of the World Test Championship table. Root’s men had appeared set for a quickfire win inside three days on Friday before debutant fast bowler Razaullah launched an audacious assault with the bat, clubbing nine sixes as he raced to 81 off 63 balls. The 21-year-old number nine, who also took four wickets in England’s first innings, put on 121 for the ninth wicket with fellow paceman Abbas (42) as England floundered. “We had a little bit of pushback yesterday which, in a strange way, was quite a good thing for the group,” said Root. “Fair play to Razaullah, he made things difficult for us. He played some wonderful shots and made it very difficult to set fields to. He struck the ball nicely – I don’t know how he didn’t pull a muscle, swinging the bat that hard.” Razaullah’s heroics have changed the mood music but they came too little, too late for Pakistan, who have endured a miserable series, losing the first Test by an innings and 103 runs and the second by 194 runs. The tourists sent seven players home after their crushing defeat in the second Test at Lord’s and brought in seven replacements, with Razaullah among them. They also sacked head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul as their tour plunged into chaos. Pakistan made four changes to their side for the third Test in Birmingham and they put up a fight despite being dismissed for a paltry 133 in their first innings. Captain Babar Azam admitted his team would have to take stock after a one-sided series. “Before we came here we had to think about different things and to decide our team,” he said. “We had a couple of changes after losing two matches. Playing in England is very difficult. We were trying to do our best in the third match. “We need to sit down and look hard at our mistakes, decide our playing XI.” The 3-0 win is a huge tonic for England, who were in turmoil just weeks ago following a series loss to New Zealand and the exits of head coach Brendon McCullum and Stokes. But tougher challenges lie ahead, starting with a Test series in South Africa in December and January, while a home Ashes looms next year.

Nadra-linked vaccination certificate mandatory for pilgrims from Sept 14. All pilgrims travelling for Hajj and Umrah from September 14 will be required to carry a vaccination certificate linked to the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra), it emerged on Saturday. The requirement was announced by Border Health Services-Pakistan (BHS-P) in a notice issued on September 7, which laid down vaccination requirements for Umrah and Hajj pilgrims. The directives issued to all chief operating officers cover pre-departure vaccinations against polio, meningitis, yellow fever and influenza. The BHS-P said that from September 14, no passenger would be allowed to travel without “Nadra-integrated” proof of vaccination. It noted that, as per the health minister’s directives, the federal Government Civil Dispensary was the only authorised centre for vaccinating international travellers going for Hajj or Umrah. To avoid any inconvenience for pilgrims, all airlines were requested to “strictly inform their travel agents that from now on, only proof of vaccination linked to Nadra will be acceptable for travel”. The BHS-P also requested station managers of all airlines to inform travel agents that Umrah pilgrims must obtain a “digital vaccine card linked to Nadra from an authorised vaccination centre” before their departure. Vaccination and online registration facilities will also be available at the airport in the next few days so passengers must reach six hours before their flight if they require vaccination at the airport. The vaccination fee will be paid through Nadra’s e-Sahulat platform. In January, Pakistan decided to enforce “strict and enhanced health surveillance” at all entry points in the country to prevent the cross-border transmission of Nipah virus.

Islamabad IG Ali Nasir Rizvi transferred, appointed NCCIA director general. The federal government on Saturday transferred BS-20 officer Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi from his post as inspector general of Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) Police and appointed him director general of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA), according to a notification issued by the Establishment Division. The notification said the transfer and appointment had been made with the approval of the federal government under Section 29(3) of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, as amended by the Prevention of Electronic Crimes (Amendment) Act, 2025, and Section 10 of the Civil Servants Act, 1973. The order takes “immediate effect and until further orders”. Under Section 29(3), the government can appoint the NCCIA chief for a non-extendable term of three years. Meanwhile, the outgoing Rizvi’s post will be filled by Captain (retd) Muhammad Sohail Chaudhry, who is currently serving “under the Government of Punjab”, according to a separate notification. Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi was appointed Islamabad IG on March 29, 2024, after having served in Punjab.

Hesson open to taking charge of Pakistan Test side. Pakistan interim head coach Mike Hesson has expressed his willingness to take up the Test coaching role on a permanent basis alongside his existing white-ball responsibilities, saying he believes the country has enough talent to make progress in the longest format. Hesson was speaking after Pakistan’s eight-wicket defeat by England in the third Test at Edgbaston on Friday, a loss that completed a 3-0 series defeat . Asked whether he would be interested in continuing as Test coach, Hesson said: “Yeah, I’ll be open to it for sure. You know, I love Test cricket and I think that there’s enough talent around the system in Pakistan that if we can provide some good direction, we can make some strides forward.” “But it’s certainly not going to happen in a game or two,” he added. “I think there is some skill there that I’d certainly be considering looking after.” Hesson was handed the interim Test coaching role less than a fortnight ago after the Pakistan Cricket Board removed Sarfaraz Ahmed following the defeat at Lord’s that sealed the series against England. The New Zealander, however, said no decision had yet been taken on his future with the Test side. “I haven’t even contemplated that at this stage,” he said. “I’ve got the Asian Games coming about a week after I get back. That’s my main focus in terms of the white ball. By the time that arrives, I’m sure we would have had some discussions about the Test team going forward.” Hesson also revealed that England had made preliminary contact with his agent while looking for a replacement for Brendon McCullum, but said the approach did not progress because of his commitment to Pakistan’s white-ball side until the 2027 World Cup. “I made it pretty clear that I’d committed to Pakistan,” he said. “I don’t really believe in getting a job to get another job. That’s not really the way I’ve ever operated.” Hesson nevertheless acknowledged that any decision on the Test coaching position would involve the PCB and selectors. “That’s a discussion that I’ll have with the selectors, and those are, in many ways, those decisions are not mine,” he said. Pakistan’s latest Test campaign ended with a familiar batting collapse in the first innings at Edgbaston, where they were bowled out for 133 after opting to bat first. They showed greater resistance in the second innings, recovering from 2-2 to post 450, but England comfortably chased down their target after Mohammad Abbas claimed two wickets in the opening over on the fourth morning. Hesson said the problems facing Pakistan’s Test side were deeper than the failures of the England series and called for greater attention to the skills required to succeed in the format. “The team hasn’t just struggled in the last week or two. It’s been a year or two in the making,” he said. “The attention to detail around basic things as a Test team needs work. That’s not just the playing 11, that’s right through the squad.” He said selection needed to focus on skills suited to Test cricket rather than simply runs and wickets. “You need players that can play high pace. You need players that can bring different elements to Test cricket,” Hesson said. “Some of those you can find in first-class cricket in terms of performance; some you have to identify skill. And I think that’s something that, in Pakistan, there’s always a lot of talk about having a lot of natural talent, and there is. At times, we have to be brave in terms of picking players that we think have those skills.” Hesson was encouraged, however, by the manner in which the team responded after arriving in Birmingham amid upheaval following the changes to the squad. “Once we arrived in Birmingham, everyone was pretty focused in terms of what lies ahead,” he said. “Some of the players have probably gone through that more than perhaps I have, and I think they adjusted pretty well.” The first morning had threatened another capitulation after Pakistan lost three wickets cheaply in the opening period. “Losing the toss and dealing with some pretty good seam bowling and handing over probably three or four soft ones in the first hour and a half created a little bit of chaos in the changing room,” Hesson said. “But outside of that, I think the boys were nice and calm and I was really pleased with the way we showed some character the last couple of days. It wasn’t perfect, but there were certainly some really good signs.” Pakistan’s next Test assignment is a two-match home series against Sri Lanka in November.

Pakistan urges UN to close gaps in fight against evolving terror threat. UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan on Saturday urged the UN Security Council to strengthen its counter-terrorism mechanisms and close gaps in sanctions regimes as a new UN assessment warned that terrorist groups were rapidly adapting their propaganda, recruitment and financing methods. The UN report specifically highlights the proscribed Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) as an example of how terrorist groups increasingly use propaganda to reinforce their operations, exploit local grievances, build legitimacy, facilitate fundraising and shape perceptions of authority. Meanwhile, more than 30 independent UN human-rights experts warned that the 25-year campaign against terrorism had also taken a heavy toll on human rights and fundamental freedoms, while stretching the boundaries of international law. The two concerns — the rapidly evolving terrorist threat and the consequences of the international response to it — dominated a Security Council discussion marking 25 years since the Sept 11 attacks . A new report by the Security Council’s Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate (CTED) said terrorist propaganda had moved far beyond messaging and had become embedded in the operational structure of terrorist groups, helping them recruit fighters, raise funds, plan operations and, in some cases, govern territory. The report specifically identified the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), along with Al Qaeda affiliate JNIM, Al-Shabaab and ISIL-K, among terrorist groups active in and around Pakistan and Afghanistan. It said terrorist groups were adapting their propaganda strategies faster than governments could respond, creating what it called an “acceleration gap” between terrorist tactics and the legislation and policies of member states. The report identified artificial intelligence, gaming platforms and alternative online spaces as among the emerging tools being exploited by terrorist organisations. It warned that young people were increasingly being targeted through social media, gaming platforms and online communities, while violent extremist groups were using graphic material and online subcultures to facilitate radicalisation. Against this backdrop, Pakistan’s Permanent Representative Asim Iftikhar Ahmad told the Council that the terrorist threat had “evolved and mutated” since the 9/11 attacks and called for stronger international cooperation to counter it. He said the Council’s existing sanctions regimes also needed to be strengthened to address gaps in the global counter-terrorism framework. Asim highlighted the growing use of artificial intelligence, drones, the dark web, virtual assets and cryptocurrencies by terrorist groups for propaganda, radicalisation, recruitment, networking, attack planning and financing. He pointed to continuing terrorist threats in Africa, the Middle East and Afghanistan, warning that extremist groups were exploiting modern technologies and cross-border networks to expand their reach. Expressing particular concern over terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, Islamabad’s envoy said more than 4,700 Pakistanis had lost their lives to terrorism over the past three years. He called for effective international action against groups including the TTP, Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) and the so-called Islamic State. Pakistan, he said, had played a frontline role in the international campaign against Al Qaeda and had paid an enormous price, with more than 90,000 Pakistanis, including civilians and security and law-enforcement personnel, killed in terrorist violence since the turn of the century. The Council observed a minute of silence for the victims of the Sept 11 attacks before members renewed calls for international cooperation against terrorism. US representative Michael Waltz recalled the 2,977 people killed in the Sept 11 attacks, including citizens from more than 90 countries, and paid tribute to the first responders who ran towards the burning World Trade Centre towers. “After all, each of us has suffered,” he said, referring to terrorist attacks carried out in different countries since 2001. He called on the international community to cut off terrorist financing, deny terrorists safe havens, enforce Security Council resolutions, share intelligence and pursue those planning attacks. British Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State Chris Elmore said the international response after 9/11 had strengthened cooperation, constrained terrorist financing, transformed border and aviation security and helped prevent attacks. He called for closer cooperation with civil society and the technology and financial sectors, including efforts to harness artificial intelligence against terrorism. But he stressed that counter-terrorism measures must comply with international law, including human-rights law. France’s UN ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont said terrorist groups were increasingly using new technologies for propaganda, recruitment and financing, effectively turning innovations developed by others against their societies. He said IS, Al Qaeda and their affiliates continued to carry out attacks across borders and called on the Security Council to renew the leadership role it had assumed after the 9/11 attacks, including by developing effective measures against terrorists’ exploitation of new technologies. Human-rights costs The anniversary discussion, however, also brought a forceful warning that the international response to terrorism must not undermine the rights and freedoms it seeks to protect. More than 30 independent UN human-rights experts said too many countries had adopted unnecessary and disproportionate responses after the Sept 11 attacks that seriously undermined human rights, civil society, civic space, democracy and the rule of law. The experts, appointed through the UN Human Rights Council but independent of the UN and unpaid for their work, said the so-called “wars on terror” had stretched foundational rules of international law “beyond their breaking point”. Worldwide monitoring over the past quarter century had exposed some of the gravest violations of international law committed in the name of countering terrorism, they said, citing wars of aggression, unlawful occupations, “countless” war crimes and crimes against humanity, as well as plausible allegations of genocide. They also highlighted assassinations presented as “targeted killings”, torture disguised as “interrogation”, secret detention, enforced disappearances and unfair military trials and special courts, including at the US-operated Guantanamo Bay detention facility. The experts urged states to review their counter-terrorism laws and practices to ensure compliance with international human rights, humanitarian and refugee law. Their warning added a second dimension to the 25-year assessment of the global campaign against terrorism: while terrorist organisations have adapted rapidly to new technologies and methods, governments must ensure that their response does not erode the fundamental rights, democratic institutions and international legal protections that the counter-terrorism campaign is intended to defend. ‘Assault on humanity’ UN Secretary-General António Guterres, in his anniversary message, described the Sept 11 attacks as “an assault on humanity itself” and paid tribute to the nearly 3,000 victims, survivors and first responders. “As we mark this sombre occasion on 11 September, we remember the nearly 3,000 victims — from the United States and more than 90 countries — and stand with their families and loved ones,” he said. Guterres noted that 2026 also marked 20 years since member states adopted the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, describing the fight against terrorism as a shared and unfinished task. “As we pay tribute to the victims, let us renew our shared commitment to build a future free from terrorism,” he said. The Security Council’s discussion came 25 years after Resolution 1373 established the Council’s counter-terrorism machinery in response to the Sept 11 attacks.

PML-N's Rana Sanaullah says Parliament to decide on more provinces. Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Saturday that Parliament will decide on the matter of creating new provinces. The recent debate regarding new provinces began in late July when Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi called for new provinces as part of reforms to the current governance system, drawing strong reactions from government ministers. During a press conference in Lahore, Sanaullah was asked about Naqvi’s recent remarks where he said that “new administrative units will eventually have to be created as Pakistan’s growing population and changing needs can no longer be effectively managed through the existing administrative structure”. The PML-N leader replied that making such statements at business seminars or conferences had not resulted in any “improvement” in the situation. “In my humble opinion, this debate should have been started in Parliament,” he said, adding that issues of such magnitude should not be reduced to speeches, social media, seminars or business forums. “The outcome will also emerge in Parliament,” the PM’s adviser said, adding that the “matter will be resolved in a better direction” when all political parties and the leadership of all provinces discuss it. “In any circumstance, the decision of whether any province will be created or not will be made in Parliament, and by Parliament,” Sanaullah reiterated. He also stressed that Naqvi, in his remarks, had said the creation of new provinces depended on whether the public wanted it . “If the public wants, then no one can stop it. The decision of whether the public wants it or not can only be made in Parliament,” the PML-N leader said. Sanaullah said his party was deliberating upon the matter and will issue a policy statement after participating in the debate and once it “comes to a proper place where a result could emerge”. The PM’s aide further said that no minister had raised the matter before the federal cabinet so far, adding that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif would issue the appropriate directives once the topic is discussed. He emphasised that even if a referendum were to be held to gauge public opinion, it would require approval by the parliament. He remarked that the PML-N was not “bound” to issue a statement on the topic of new provinces merely based on economic forums. Referring to the Sindh Assembly’s adoption of a resolution against dividing the province, Sanaullah said the PPP had “overreacted”. Coalition partners to resolve differences Speaking on the recent rift between the PPP and the PML-N, the minister said differences between the two parties had, by and large, been resolved. Sanaullah, who is also a member of the core committees formed to resolve differences between the two major coalition partners, said after attending a meeting at Governor House that any remaining issues would be settled amicably, as both sides were committed to resolving them. “Ideally, the core committees should meet every month, but this could not happen due to the elections in GB and AJK. Meetings will now hopefully be held more regularly to smooth over any old or new rough patches,” he said. He attributed the tensions mainly to emotionally charged election campaigns in Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir , saying the campaigns were now over and so were the frictions. The PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre, has strongly opposed the suggested move to carve out Karachi as a separate province. PML-N’s Khawaja Asif, who had earlier noted that the appropriate forum for such a discussion was the parliament, said last week that devolution of power was “ inevitable ”. The opposition parties, including the PTI, have said they will hold consultations to call an all-parties conference to discuss several issues, including the creation of new provinces, law and order and the economy. PTI, JI marches to Islamabad Asked about the plans of the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and the PTI to march towards Islamabad on September 20 and 27, respectively, Sanaullah remarked that the JI’s past political activities had been peaceful while the same could not be expected from the PTI. “Everyone knows that JI is a political party and it has always carried out its activities according to the Constitutional and legal requirements,” he said. He affirmed that the government “respected” political protests and therefore had held negotiations with the JI during which its representatives “carefully and seriously listened to their demands”. The PM’s adviser urged JI leaders not to “overwork themselves needlessly” as the PML-N and PM Shehbaz also wanted a reduction in the fuel prices and electricity bills “as much as and even more than JI did”. On the other hand, Sanaullah said the government had “no expectation” that the PTI’s long march would remain peaceful and referred to remarks made by its leaders. “If they are coming to Islamabad to overthrow the government and if this is their intention and thinking, then it is obvious that they will carry out violence after coming there,” he asserted. “Based on these reports, our assessment is that it could be a replay of May 9. If it takes that route and assumes a similar proportion, it would be very unfortunate. Since the matter is also before the courts, the government is awaiting their decisions before finalising its strategy. But one thing is certain: violence cannot be allowed,” he said. Additional input from Ahmed Faraz

Anthropic boss calls for AI slowdown, Altman and Musk agree. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence (AI) firms to slow down the development of the powerful technology, amid mounting worries over the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems. His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “ gambling with our lives ” in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement. OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI, quickly chimed in to say they agreed with Amodei’s assessment, as pressure builds for improved oversight. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website . “Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way,” said Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021. “But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence.” Amodei’s statement echoed another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development. Then in late July, Altman said developers might need to voluntarily tap the brakes to give society a chance to catch up. More than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies, including Anthropic, signed a petition calling on the US government to help “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” OpenAI had revealed that during testing, AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code. In that incident and others, the blame was placed on AI agents, which are software programs that can carry out tasks without constant supervision by humans. “Dario is right,” Musk wrote on X, as Altman said: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.” ‘Gambling with our lives’ Earlier this week, Coxon, 27, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pretraining AI models — first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach. Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said in a post on X on Tuesday. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence. ‘Taking over the entire internet’ Amodei cautioned that the Hugging Face incident should not be dismissed as a one-off. “A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand,” he explained. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” potentially generating hundreds of billions of dollars in damage, he added. The Anthropic CEO said his company would grant “employee-like access” to a team of “third-party evaluators” who would verify adherence to safety practices — and he called on all companies to follow his lead. Altman said he would commit to similar outside oversight, adding that he would have “more to share soon.” Amodei also suggested that companies work together to establish common safety standards, and said he supported some kind of government cooperation on the issue. In early August, the US government put in place a voluntary security review process for advanced AI models before their release, but the parameters of that program remain unclear. Industry observers say they are not sure how effective it would be, as President Donald Trump’s administration has thus far favoured a light-touch, deregulatory approach to most industries, including tech.

Tens of thousands protest against far right in Germany. Tens of thousands of protesters took part in demonstrations across Germany on Saturday against the far-right AfD, after the party scored a crushing victory in a state election last week. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) topped the vote in the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt, and is now seeking to form the first extreme-right state government in Germany since World War II. About 150,000 demonstrators took to the streets in around 20 cities nationwide, including Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, in protests that were called by Pruef, which advocates for a ban on the AfD, organisers said. They waved signs emblazoned with slogans that read “Ban the AfD now,” and “Democracy needs no alternatives”. A counter-protester holds a sign reading “Who replaces remigrated caregivers” during a final election campaign rally of far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party ahead of Berlin’s state election in Germany on September 12, 2026. — AFP “A broad cross-section of civil society is taking to the streets to prevent the enemies of the constitution, the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, from gaining government power,” said Christoph Bautz, head of campaign group Campact, also involved in the demonstrations. The rise of the AfD has unnerved many who feel Germany has a special responsibility to atone for its Nazi past, and calls have grown for mainstream parties to seek to ban the group. But hurdles for a formal ban are high in Germany, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, of the centre-right CDU party, remains sceptical about taking such an approach. In Berlin, police said several thousand protesters took part in several demonstrations. The AfD held a counter-demonstration in the capital, attended by Kristin Brinker, its lead candidate in next weekend’s regional elections in Berlin. Campact said there were around 25,000 demonstrators in Hamburg and 12,000 in Munich. The anti-immigration, Russia-friendly party took almost 44 per cent of the vote in last Sunday’s election in Saxony-Anhalt, against 17pc for the CDU. It fell three seats short of an absolute majority and has started talks with other groups and MPs in an effort to form a state government.

Pakistan, African countries eye $15bn trade by 2030. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and African countries at the inaugural ceremony of the Pakistan-Africa Economic Council (PAEC) reaffirmed their resolve to raise bilateral trade to $15 billion by 2030, diversify economic and trade relations, and bring the private sectors, including chambers of commerce from both sides, closer to each other. The two sides also reiterated their commitment to promoting mutual investment and, through comprehensive and long-term planning, fully exploiting their untapped resources to take bilateral economic and trade relations to new heights. The inaugural ceremony featured detailed discussions on promoting trade, investment, economic cooperation and business ties between Pakistan and African nations. Ambassadors, high commissioners and consuls general from various African countries, including Rwanda, Mauritius, Morocco, Zimbabwe, Sudan, Kenya and Ethiopia, attended the ceremony. The speakers highlighted key Pakistani sectors, including agriculture, textiles, pharmaceuticals, information technology, minerals and mining, technology, food, education and infrastructure, that offer significant trade and investment potential in Africa, emphasising that both regions should leverage their large populations, resources and expansive markets. Federal Minister for Defence Production Raza Hayat Hiraj said the forum would play a great role in enhancing economic and trade ties between African countries and Pakistan, describing it as a milestone in the economic history of both sides. He said Africa’s population of 1.5 billion represented huge potential for Pakistan and that the private sector's role was significant in increasing economic and trade ties. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said the forum would work to strengthen economic and trade relations between Pakistan and the African region. He said Africa had a great future, adding that a rising Africa and an emerging Pakistan had huge potential for growth. PAEC Patron-in-Chief Hamid Asgher Khan said Africa was a “slumbering giant” that was awakening and would play a huge role in the global geo-economy, while economic and trade connectivity with Pakistan and other potential economies could further strengthen the relationship. Mr Khan said bilateral trade between the African region and Pakistan was far below its true potential and there was a huge need to increase bilateral trade to $15 billion in the coming years to exploit its true potential. He said Pakistan's current economic and trade potential in IT stood at $2.7bn and could double after stronger connectivity with the African region in the coming years. Published in Dawn, September 13th, 2026

Beyond the bale: Can Pakistan’s cotton sector be rebuilt from the ground up?. Pakistan’s cotton sector has long been the backbone of the country’s economy. The textile industry contributes roughly eight percent to national GDP and provides livelihoods for nearly 10 million people. But the crop that once powered Pakistan’s economy is now in deep crisis. In 2004, Pakistan produced more than 14 million bales of cotton. Two decades later, national output has fallen to between 4.8 and 5.6 million bales, depending on the season — a decline of roughly 60 to 70 percent from its peak. The decline has several interconnected causes. Farmers are increasingly abandoning cotton because of poor yields, volatile prices and competition from crops such as sugarcane and rice. More than 90pc of Pakistan’s roughly 1.5 million cotton farmers cultivate less than five hectares, making it difficult to afford modern machinery, improved techniques or absorb losses from a bad season. The effectiveness of Bt cotton, which dominates Pakistan’s cotton cultivation, has also declined, leaving farmers increasingly exposed to pests such as pink bollworm. Heatwaves, erratic rainfall and water shortages have added further pressure, particularly in Sindh. The crisis is also a crisis of livelihoods. An International Labour Organisation study found widespread labour exploitation across the cotton supply chain, including inadequate wages, insecure employment and limited social protection. Women perform much of the manual work but face barriers to training, resources and decision-making. Child labour also remains common. Several initiatives are attempting to reverse the decline. The Better Cotton Initiative (BCI), the world’s largest cotton sustainability programme, promotes better practices in pesticide use, water efficiency, soil health, biodiversity and decent work. In Pakistan, the National Rural Support Programme (NRSP), through the Rural Support Programmes Network, has been implementing a BCI project in Dera Ghazi Khan since March 2025. The project has registered 6,000 small cotton farmers, 20pc of them women, cultivating 16,000 acres. Farmers have received training, soil testing, demonstration plots and guidance on climate-resilient seed varieties, bio-pesticides, mulching and laser levelling. An external audit in early 2026 assessed the registered farmers against BCI standards, resulting in a Permission to Trade certificate that enables their cotton to be traded with approved ginners. Such certification can help connect farmers with international buyers increasingly demanding traceable and sustainably produced cotton. However, certification alone cannot solve the sector’s deeper problems. The 6,000 farmers covered by the project represent only a fraction of the country’s 1.5 million cotton farmers. Farmers still struggle with seed quality, water scarcity, affordable credit, mechanisation and market access. Finance may be the most critical missing link. Smallholders often depend on informal lenders and cannot afford the inputs, machinery or working capital needed to benefit fully from training and certification. Credit and certification therefore need to move together. Pakistan’s cotton revival will require coordinated action by government, agriculture departments, financial institutions, ginners, textile manufacturers and development organisations. Affordable credit, mechanisation, climate-smart technology, stronger seed regulation, better water management and realistic pricing policies must advance together. The Dera Ghazi Khan project demonstrates that training, farmer field schools and certification can work at pilot scale. The challenge now is to take these lessons to the 1.5 million farmers outside such programmes. Pakistan’s cotton sector is in crisis, but it is not beyond recovery. What it needs is investment and coordination at the scale the crisis demands. The author is a climate researcher and development specialist. Published in Dawn, September 13th, 2026

Pakistan has potential to become international arbitration hub: LHC judge. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan is well-positioned to emerge as a preferred seat of international arbitration be­­cause of substantial cost benefits and prevailing geopolitical goodwill, said Justice Jawad Hassan of the Lahore High Court’s Rawalpindi bench. “Pakistan is making good progress on infrastructure and laws on arbitration and mediation as there is a large demand for commercial arbitration and mediation,” Justice Hassan said while speaking at a seminar titled “Can Pakistan Become a Seat of International Dispute Resolution?” at the Islamabad Policy Research Institute (IPRI). Justice Hassan added that the pending judgement in the Star Hydro case would set the stage for further progress in this regard. Former Punjab advocate general Asma Hamid, Barrister Salahuddin Ahmed of MCA Law Associates, Brig (retd) Raja Shozab Majeed, Deputy Director and Chair of the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators (CIArb) Pakistan, Feisal Naqvi of BNR, Barrister Mian Sheraz Javed, Chair of CIArb, and eminent international lawyer Ahmer Bilal Soofi participated in the discussion. Country’s arbitration capacity expands as case law, mediators grow Senior jurists, advocates and arbitration specialists brainstormed on whether Pakistan could establish itself as a venue for international arbitration and mediation. A broad consensus emerged that while the potential exists, realising this vision would require sustained, decade-long strategic collaboration across the legal and institutional sectors. The panel was unanimous that Pakistan had a genuine opportunity to become an international arbitration hub, but only through sustained legal and institutional reforms and capacity-building over the coming decade. Building the arbitration ecosystem It was noted that as Pakistan expanded trade and attracted investment through projects such as CPEC, most of its commercial disputes were still heard abroad in London, Singapore or Dubai, making the country a consumer rather than a provider of arbitration services, at considerable cost in terms of money, time and confidence. Speakers observed that each international arbitration typically costs parties no less than two to three million pounds or dollars. They also pointed to Pakistan’s recent emergence as an international mediator, including its hosting of US-Iran talks in Islamabad, as evidence of a credibility that could be extended to commercial dispute resolution. Speakers stressed that some of the foundations were already in place. Pakistan is a party to the New York Convention, meaning awards made domestically can be enforced internationally, while its courts have deve­­loped a clear pro-enforcement appro­ach towards foreign arbitral awards. The panel noted the striking growth in relevant case law. While the arbitration framework, which still rests on the 1940 Act, produced only 56 reported judgements two years ago, arbitration-related judgements are now emerging at a rate of around 120. It was also noted that Pakistan is one of only seven countries in the world with a mandatory mediation regime. Mediation has already saved substantial public money, including more than Rs1 trillion through settlements with independent power producers and a recent $6.6 billion refinery upgrade deal. The discussion also highlighted Pakistan’s rapidly expanding pool of arbitrators. The number has grown from six to eight just two years ago to nearly 100 fellows of the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators today, compared with roughly 150 in Singapore, 39 in the UAE and 42 in India. COMMENT: Razaullah and Pakistan cricket’s lost soul. Edgbaston 2026. A phoenix rises from the ashes. Remember this. Do not forget it. When the house of Pakistan cricket is burning to a crisp, an unknown man called Razaullah stands tall with pride, passion, and fire. He stands in the true spirit of Pakistan cricket. This is no odyssey but it is Hollywood. Half Shahid Afridi, half Wasim Akram, this former nobody from Mardan reminds us that cricket is a game of waiting for a miracle — and sometimes you feel its joy. Pakistan’s happiest day of a horrible Test series arrived at the last. It was a day of gritty and positive batting. Shan Masood, Babar Azam, and Azan Awais contributed. It was a day that ensured Mohammad Abbas would remember this tour more for his batting than his bowling. It was a day for everyone who had clung to their love for the true spirit of Pakistan cricket. But above all, it was the day of Razaullah of Mardan. The next day, the final of the series , however exposed the chronic failings in the bowling attack, something that a raw talent like Razaullah had no hope of overcoming. A 3-0 defeat is both disappointing and deserved. Pakistan’s miserable failure in England is a failure of preparation. The causal pathway to that explanation is insanely complicated and spans generations. The players have played their part, but the players are only a product of the cricket system and the broader society that creates them. We made them, we must own their failure, and we must play our part in remaking their souls, their spirit, and their success. The rookie all-rounder from Mardan offers a glimpse of the raw, fearless spirit that once made Pakistan cricket great What we will remember of this series is the cricketing incompetence of Mohsin Naqvi’s Pakistan Cricket Board. Mess at the top A great deal has already been written and spoken on this matter. When this much mess piles up no doubt the man at the top is to blame. The solution is well known and nothing new: the PCB must be run by independent, professional administrators, not glory-seeking politicians and egotistical former cricketers. The discovery of Razaullah, the one swallow of this English summer, does not get Naqvi off the hook. Pakistan’s political leadership must construct the cricket system in the best interests of the country. If that were to happen tomorrow, it will still take a decade to bring Pakistan cricket back to the top table. As a political leader, why wouldn’t you want to make the people happy and bring glory back to your country? Don’t wait, start now. Premature obituary Some scribes have already written the obituary of Pakistan cricket, but the reason that obituary should remain on hold was in full evidence on the third day of the Edgbaston Test. At the threshold of defeat, a smile on his raw face, Razaullah smashed a record number of sixes on Test debut. He made an absolute mockery of Pakistan’s previous batting form and attitude. He took his country from the inevitability of an innings defeat to a wild dream of victory. The smile on Razaullah’s face transferred to the smiles of spectators and viewers. The uninhibited defiance of his batting transferred to the willow of his doughty batting partner, Abbas, who too suddenly smashed cricket balls. The legend of Razaullah had already emerged. His debut bowling over, which topped 90mph and trapped Joe Root lbw, engraved Razaullah’s name in the book of eternal debuts. But he did something more, something beautifully and unexpectedly timed: he showed the world, including his country’s administrators, the formula that made Pakistan cricket great. He bowled with high pace and aggression — albeit lacking consistency. He batted with positivity and freedom. Most importantly, he held his head high, fought fire with fire, and played for his country’s pride. It’s a formula that makes Pakistan inconsistent, but it also once made them brilliant. It’s a formula that, if you can get it to work more often than not, will propel you back to the top. The second innings at Edgbaston went some way towards proving that this was a batting line-up of sufficient experience and promise not to have crumbled as it did in the series. The batsmen underperformed because the system makes them unready, physically and mentally, to succeed consistently at elite level. The talent is there; it needs nurturing and developing. But the PCB doesn’t get that. Razaullah is a hero today, he may be gone tomorrow. Pakistan won their first Test series in England in 1987. It was a wet summer that didn’t particularly suit Pakistan, but Imran Khan’s uprising was in full flow. That series win was a natural progression, an expected step up the ladder of international credibility. Pakistan dominated England for the next two decades until England’s infamous series win of 2006. By a quirk of statistics, Pakistan haven’t won a Test series in England since 1996. That was the first series I covered as a cricket writer and Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis were in full cry. What a sight they were, dismantling the opposition with the gusto of champions. Decline mystifying What has happened to Pakistan cricket since is too complex, too unfathomable, and too painful to relate here. But for the Gen-Zs who will inherit the Earth, know this: we once were kings. Today, Pakistan loses on the cricket pitch and in cricket politics. It loses in administration and finances. It loses in the hearts and minds of the global audience which this country of mercurial geniuses attracted in its glory days. The last grains of that magic dust have been drifting away over two decades. What was once the electrifying ebb and flow of Pakistan’s version of cricket became a fading spell. In this ebbing English summer, the Pakistan cricket show was a media gift from heaven. It sparked a spiralling series of hyperbolic condemnations. If you divide the current Test nations into two divisions, Paki­stan, a fallen power, will battle for the top of division two. But why do we still watch, and hope, after two decades of demise? The answer to that question is Razaullah of Mardan and Pakistan. For all the dog days of this series and recent years, we live for days like these, when an unjaded soul shows the world what Pakistan cricket and Pakistan can truly be. State Bank in tight spot as inflation rises. KARACHI: Pakistan and other regional states are unable to adopt a clear position on economic and monetary policies due to the prolonged Gulf war , which has driven up fuel prices, according to researchers and analysts. An increase in inflation in 2026-27 and a global trend of higher interest rates have also forced the State Bank of Pakistan to take cautious steps regarding the policy rate to be announced at the next meeting of the monetary committee on Monday. The current interest rate is 11.5 per cent, but trade and industry think it is high compared to competitive markets. Bankers anticipate a status quo, but some analysts believe the central bank will lift its policy rate by 50 basis points at the Monetary Policy Committee meeting. Institutional traders expect 50bps rate hike; analysts see status quo The SBP raised its policy rate to 11.5pc by 100bps on April 27 in response to rising global energy prices and supply chain risks. As the war in the Gulf expands to the Red Sea, fuel prices have shot above $100 as constant attacks have made it impossible for oil tankers to cross the route. Some analysts said the State Bank is in a difficult position on tightening its monetary policy stance amid rising inflation. However, the SBP is believed to prefer maintaining the status quo. It may be about everybody else’s inflation problem,” said Faisal Mamsa, CEO of Tresmark. For instance, the global markets are going awry. Brent is above $105, the ECB (European Central Bank) has raised rates by 25bps, global bond yields have surged, and US inflation remains elevated around the 3.4pc mark. “None of these problems started in Pakistan, but the SBP may increasingly have to respond to them,” he said. A poll conducted by Tresmark on Wednesday showed 20pc of institutional traders expecting a 50bps rate hike in Monday’s MPC. “Two weeks ago, we stated that the status quo was probably the best-case scenario for the September MPC. We still think it is,” said Mr Mamsa. Bloomberg Economics and BMI have now moved to a similar view, expecting no change on Monday but growing upward pressure on rates going forward. Pakistan: 25 years post-2001. THE terrorist events of Sept 11, 2001, changed the world and brought about a new security order. Social engineering took place on a large scale, especially within Muslim societies. Conflict erupted across Africa and Asia, often linked to terrorism. These developments triggered large-scale migration towards the West and strengthened the far right in Western societies. Populism took multiple forms. In short, the world changed course, and an era of increasingly controlled societies emerged, affecting technology, the economy, mobility and politics. The 25th anniversary of the tragic incident has triggered a debate: what has the world gained and lost since these events, and what kind of world em­­erged in their aftermath? This question is equally important for Pakistan, as it became a front-line state in the global war against terrorism. Pakistan’s 25-year experience can perhaps be summarised in one sentence: the country has fai­led to defeat terrorism completely, lost Afgha­nis­tan, witnessed weakened internal cohesion, experienced the rise of authoritarianism, and its economy remains in disarray. The return of the Taliban to power in Afghanistan in 2021 contributed to renewed challenges, particularly from the banned TTP . Meanwhile, Balochistan remains another major security theatre, with separatist groups targeting security forces, infrastructure, and Chinese interests. Economically, Pakistan received billions of dollars in US assistance and Coalition Support Funds but failed to convert this geopolitical opportunity into lasting economic transformation. Terrorism imposed enormous costs through loss of life, reduced investment, damaged infrastructure, and increased security expenditure. However, Pakistan has also achieved significant strategic successes. Before 9/11, Pakistan was under sanctions because of its nuclear tests. The Kargil conflict had contributed to political instability and military rule, and Pakistan experienced some global isolation. After September 2001, however, Pakistan emerged from isolation to become a front-line ally of the US in its global ‘war on terror’. Pakistan was later designated a major non-Nato ally. However, this partnership came to be characterised by mistrust, particular­ly over Afghanistan, terrorist sanctuaries, drone strikes, and the 2011 Abbottabad operation. The country’s biggest achievements and major failures have been in counterterrorism. Pakistan’s biggest achievements and major failures have been in counterterrorism. Through operations including Rah-i-Raast, Rah-i-Nijaat, Zarb-i-Azb , and Raddul Fasaad, Pakistan dismantled major terrorist sanctuaries. It ended the ability of terrorist groups to exercise territorial control in areas such as Swat and the former tribal districts. In foreign relations, Pakistan strengthened its strategic partnership with China and expanded ties with the Gulf countries and Türkiye, but its relations with Afghanistan have remained deeply problematic. While it took nearly two decades to fully abandon the use of radical and militant proxies on the external and internal political fronts, two factors played an important role. First, international pressure forced the establishment to take measures against militant groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed. Second, many members of such groups became disillusioned and joined the TTP, Al Qaeda, and IS-K, making it increasingly difficult for security operators to treat and manage these networks separately. Although these groups are no longer openly active in militancy, they still shoulder political and diplomatic baggage. India frequently exploits this issue to confront Pakistan at the diplomatic level and has used it to build pressure against Pakistan, contributing directly to the military confrontation last year. However, the international community increasingly recognises Pakistan’s efforts to overcome its terrorism problem, and India’s terrorism narrative against Pakistan appears to be losing some of its effectiveness internationally. Over the last 25 years, terrorism has emerged as a core problem for the country, while counterterrorism has become one of its key strengths. Pakistan remains among the countries most affected by terrorism . Security concerns have negatively impacted Pakistan-China relations, especially CPEC. At the same time, counterterrorism has provided an avenue for cooperation between the US and Pakistan, and since President Donald Trump took office, the two have developed greater synergy against IS-K and in dealing with the Taliban, apart from their multilevel engagement in the Gulf region. In this re-engagement, Pakistan has lost the strategic vision for Afghanistan that Gen Ziaul Haq and his predecessors had crafted. Terrorism and counterterrorism have changed the country’s structure. Counterterrorism has created an imbalance of power, as civilian governments gradually handed over internal and external security affairs to the establishment and re­­frained from interfering in order to avoid friction. As a result, political engineering became more convenient for the establishment. Social and political engineering have also changed society and left it without direction. Terrorism remai­­ns a major obstacle to attracting foreign investment into the country, yet Pakistan’s counterterrorism capabilities have become a strength that allows it to engage with Western and Asian countries. From Gen Pervez Musharraf onwards, military leaders have tried to take credit for the counterterrorism efforts. Yet it is paradoxical that very few acknowledged terrorism as an indigenous problem rooted partly in previous state policies of nurturing militant proxies. In alliance with the clergy, these policies created an infrastructure of extremism in the country. Religious groups were used for multiple purposes — from advancing nationalist projects to acting as pressure groups. Their perception of terrorism was simplistic, and simplistic approaches produced poor policies and flawed strategies. During these years, Pakistan lost 75,366 people, including 3,189 soldiers, 2,598 FC personnel, 3,599 police officers, and 26,547 civilians, apart from casualties in other security institutions. Pakistan launched 2,961 military operations, both medium- and large-scale, against terrorists, in addition to several other types of military operations against terrorism. The country has established dedicated counterterrorism institutions, including Nacta (lately in the news for another reason), counter-extremism centres, NFTIC, and others. Pakistan has also produced 13 policy documents, ranging from the National Action Plan and National Security Policy to Paigham-i-Pakistan. After all these sacrifices, operations, institutions, and policy documents, is Pakistan still searching for a new counterterrorism policy? The writer is a security analyst.
