A Stopgap Peace A major challenge to peace in the Bangsamoro is the fact that security forces remain unable to stem the horizontal violence that plagues the region. The problem persists in part because they tend to manage localised conflicts rather than resolve them, leaving space for violence to resurface. When clashes erupt, in some cases violence continues for hours before the military, which is typically the first responder, steps in. Beyond the physical dangers that communities face, these experiences undermine public perceptions of the armed forces, and more generally of what peace should entail. 130 Crisis Group interview, source from Lanao region, Manila, 8 May 2026. The military has tried to develop more flexible rules of engagement that allow for the immediate separation of warring parties, resorting to force if necessary. These guidelines, however, have not been applied consistently. Typically, the military manages to strike a ceasefire between the clashing parties, but as it does not have the mandate to resolve the issue that triggered the violence, the conflict often reignites further down the line. A vital element in these arrangements is often the payment of “blood money”, a form of compensation offered following an individual’s violent death. Some politicians, and even members of the MILF rank and file, have come to view this practice as harmful, since payment offers no guarantee that the conflict will cease. There are other obstacles to hammering out durable ceasefires. As conflicts tend to spill over village and town boundaries, a broader solution dealing with root causes in several municipalities, such as land ownership disputes, would be preferable. Municipal governments, however, often struggle to cooperate, which means this approach often is not feasible. 131 Crisis Group interview, former regional official, Cotabato City, 12 February 2026. In addition, regional ministries sometimes apply “ready made” solutions they have already successfully tested elsewhere, without taking into account the local context of the feud they are dealing with. 132 Crisis Group interview, MILF leaders, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. This has occurred, for example, in Maguindanao. There were also cases where no ministerial intervention followed at all and local people resolved the conflict on their own. Even the MILF is not always able to resolve feuds beyond achieving a ceasefire. 133 In one case, a MILF commander around the MILF camp Abubakar hesitated to resolve a land issue between two of his followers and advised the village to take care of it. There was, however, no follow-up. Crisis Group interview, land experts, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Furthermore, a local non-governmental organisation noted that “infrequent and unstructured” peace dialogues most often fail to include women, young people with disabilities and non-Moro Indigenous people. 134 Moro Women Development and Cultural Center, Inc., “From Consultation to Action – Advancing Peace Together”, Summary Report, Peace Conference 2025, Davao City, 4 December 2025, p. 30. In some instances, this lack of inclusivity has perpetuated feuding or revived land conflicts that had otherwise been considered as resolved. V. Pathways to Local Stability Addressing the complexity of local conflict in the Bangsamoro cannot be done through a single sweeping reform. Rather, it requires a series of careful adjustments across institutions. 135 Crisis Group interviews, police, military and local Bangsamoro officials, January-March 2026. Focusing only on the police or the judiciary is unlikely to produce the desired results, which is why regional stability hinges on a combination of different policies. Police outpost in Cotabato City, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht A. Improving Security Coordination As the Bangsamoro stabilises, Manila has an opportunity to reorient its military toward external defence and set the foundation for the police to take the lead in managing day-to-day security in the region. While a full handover of responsibilities would be premature, the military and regional police can start formulating a plan to do so in the near future. 136 Crisis Group interview, police commission official, 12 February 2026. The existing Joint Peace and Security Coordinating Center (mentioned in Section IV.B) could be strengthened to take on this task. The centre should, for example, design more joint operations and establish a roadmap for regional and provincial security powers to be passed from the military to the police. Consolidating regional security will require a redistribution of state forces, while ensuring Mindanao retains a baseline military presence. 137 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, Manila, June-July 2024. The government should increase the police’s responsibilities in the region’s more stable areas, pairing this move with a gradual drawdown of military units. Mobile army platoons or detachments should deploy to volatile hotspots, including parts of Maguindanao del Sur, the mountainous corridor between Maguindanao and Lanao, and areas where non-Moro Indigenous communities live. To offset these small-unit redeployments, troops from the region’s flanks, such as the southern Visayas or eastern Mindanao, should shift to conflict-affected areas within the Bangsamoro in order to concentrate the military where it can maximise stability. Lastly, it is vital to deepen existing but modest military and police collaboration in Central Mindanao, through intelligence-sharing, joint training, and coordinated non-combat operations. 138 Crisis Group interview, senior military official, 16 February 2025. It is also crucial for the military to re-examine the rationale for auxiliary forces. In some areas that do not see conflict, some CAFGU paramilitary units should be demobilised. More broadly, better oversight of these forces is essential: commanders should apply strict accountability and disciplinary measures, and sanction transgressions. 139 Crisis Group interview, former military officer, Manila, 29 May 2024. In the long run, the Philippine government’s objective should be to dismantle all state-backed militias in a phased manner and rely only on professional forces. B. Reforming Regional Policing Reforming policing arrangements in a complex environment while remaining respectful of both the Philippine constitution and the Bangsamoro’s autonomous status will be difficult. As mentioned previously, Crisis Group takes the view that a Bangsamoro police force outside the realm of the national police is not practical at this stage. A more prudent approach in the short term is to reform the existing law enforcement set-up. 140 Crisis Group interviews, Lanao, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. To that end, police stations must be resourced with the equipment they need. The national government should also hire more officers so as to boost the police-to-population ratio. Authorities could reassign qualified officers currently posted in peaceful areas outside the Bangsamoro to the region. They also could increase the recruitment of MILF and MNLF fighters into the regular police force, starting with those who passed the test but were never hired. Expanding the ranks of Moro officers would foster trust with both the MILF and with communities that still view the police with suspicion. Ensuring ex-rebel recruits receive proper training and mentoring, and are fully acquainted with the communities they serve, will be essential to prepare officers and cadets. Foreign donors involved with the peace process could support such initiatives with training design and funding. Adjustments in police operations could also help build a more credible force. Once it has the numbers and skills to do so effectively, the police should strengthen targeted deterrence in hotspots where clan feuds and community violence proliferate, combining surveillance, mediation and enforcement. It should also improve its intelligence gathering, including more information-sharing between police units and more efforts to question militants and individuals involved in feuding to understand the local drivers of conflict. Stepping up community policing would ... narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. Stepping up community policing would also narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. 141 Crisis Group interviews, police and regional government officials, Maguindanao and Lanao, February 2026. The regional police force should organise a new department that would recruit, train and deploy community safety officers. 142 Funding could come from the national or the regional budget, or a combination thereof. It should, however, bypass local governments and exclude their funding to prevent them from exerting undue influence. These would ideally be recruited among demobilised MILF rebels, and would be tasked with engaging local leaders and communities and conducting visible and non-confrontational patrols. They could also aid in criminal investigations. Before rolling this out across the Bangsamoro, Manila and the regional government could run a pilot project in some municipalities with independent monitoring of its progress. Here again, foreign donors could support such programs with targeted interventions. Lastly, to restore public trust, regional leaders should combat police corruption by enforcing existing regulations. The internal affairs service and other accountability bodies should reinforce such efforts through robust oversight. Tightening procurement and inventory controls is also essential to safeguard firearms and ammunition and prevent costly – and potentially dangerous – losses. C. Breaking Conflict Cycles Security reforms are vital, but quelling violence in the region will also require addressing longstanding conflicts. Regional and national authorities should strive to make local peace deals more durable and ensure stricter adherence to the rule of law. Curbing the proliferation of firearms will necessarily be part of that process. 1. Sustainable conflict resolution Tackling horizontal violence requires de-escalating tensions when they arise, preventing them from re-erupting, and addressing root causes through conflict resolution. To prevent local quarrels from morphing into full-blown firefights, security forces need to step in as early as possible. The army, police and MILF structures all have a role to play. While the military remains best equipped to quell firefights, particularly those involving clashing MILF (and possibly MNLF) factions, internal rifts within a single MILF unit are best mediated by the ex-rebels themselves. In case of minor incidents, relying on the mediation of trusted community figures would also help avoid escalation. Effective conflict resolution in the Bangsamoro should also reach beyond the rapid responses needed once violence breaks out to address the underlying causes of conflict. Initial ceasefire agreements should include clear protocols, including sanction mechanisms, laying out the next steps in case the conflict parties violate the terms of the agreement. Once ceasefires are in place, they require rigorous monitoring, whether through the deployment of nearby police and military units, or through the participation of informal community watchers – a mechanism that has already proved successful, for example last year in the case of some feuds in Datu Saudi Ampatuan and Mamasapano towns. 143 Crisis Group interviews, local mediators, Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. 2. Building inclusive justice The police may be the “first face of justice”, but the broader judicial sector needs to be reformed as well. 144 “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, op. cit., p. 18. A first task is to strengthen the courts. This should happen through better staffing and the provision of security guarantees for judges and prosecutors, particularly when it comes to accessing remote areas. Public Sharia courts also need more support, which could come in the form of training for MILF members who are currently judges in their respective communities, but wish to practice in public courts as counsellors. 145 Sharia counsellors are individuals who passed a Sharia legal exam administered by the Supreme Court. They can represent clients and practice law at public Sharia courts. Increasing the number of so-called “mobile courts” – whereby representatives of the judiciary visit far-flung areas where there are no tribunals – would also strengthen the standing of the judiciary. In the same spirit, the regional government should broaden access to the justice system for its most vulnerable citizens by subsidising legal fees and travel expenses for community members who need to go to court. 146 Crisis Group interview, legal official, Cotabato City, 5 August 2026. Encouraging state institutions to coordinate more closely with bodies engaging in customary practices such as community mediation would also increase the efficacy of the justice system. Courts and other institutions such as village justice systems can reap the benefit of these customary practices by formally recognising not just traditional mediators, but also the actual settlement agreements reached thanks to them. 3. Navigating the firearms conundrum Dealing with the proliferation of weapons is also imperative. To begin with, the government and the MILF should restart the decommissioning of firearms. Getting the MILF back onboard with this process requires the government to deliver the support it promised demobilised fighters in the 2014 peace accord. 147 The Annex on Normalisation stipulates that in exchange for disarmament, the national government will implement a variety of other measures including compensation for demobilised fighters and the economic development of MILF camps. Given the need for the government and the MILF to rebuild trust and overcome the current stalemate, a realistic timeline will require that the process continue after the September 2026 parliamentary elections. Beyond the MILF’s weapons, the government should address gun violence in Mindanao. That begins with getting a better picture of the number of firearms in circulation. In addition to credible estimates of guns in the hands of insurgents and ex-rebels, the military and police need updated inventories of firearms issued to police and military auxiliaries, as well as clear guidelines on the storage and safeguarding of their weapons so that leaks do not occur in the first place. The state should also disarm police or members of military auxiliaries who take part in conflicts or abuse their power, and dismiss them. For their part, national agencies must tighten controls on smuggling, imports and domestic manufacture of illegal guns, as well as strengthen oversight of gun licensing and weapon registration. Across all interventions, authorities should prioritise the confiscation of high-calibre firearms, given how lethal they can be. Deterring actual gun use is also critical. Establishing a highly visible and competent police presence should serve as the foundation for these efforts. To maximise impact, these police deployments ought to be combined with strict firearm bans across the region in the lead up to elections, when gun violence tends to peak. 148 The police said that until early August they arrested twelve persons for violating the gun ban. Joviland Rita, “PNP: 12 arrested for violating BARMM election gun ban”, GMA News , 3 August 2026. Authorities should also impose penalties not only on those who possess unlicensed firearms but also those who manufacture, store or use them for political ends. Religious leaders and clan elders can also contribute to eradicating the excesses of Bangsamoro’s gun culture by mounting campaigns to rectify the belief that the use of firearms beyond self-defence is legitimate. 149 Crisis Group interviews, local civil society, Cotabato and Marawi, February-March 2026. VI. Conclusion Armed rebellions have tailed off across the southern Philippines, but the peace they have given way to is constantly threatened by clan warfare, political volatility and factional disputes within the former insurgent MILF. The architects of the Bangsamoro peace agreement saw reforms to the police force, backed by improvements in institutions handling conflict resolution and justice, as a way to propel the region from war to peace. Yet a series of obstacles has slowed police reform and prevented institutions from maintaining law and order. Manila and the Bangsamoro government will need to work in tandem and be realistic about proposed reforms. A law enforcement system that is competent, representative and fair, and which can earn public trust by making communities safer, is an essential step forward. A more effective and accessible judicial system, as well as moves to tighten gun control and ensure that peacebuilding initiatives address the social and political undercurrent that lead to fighting, are also vital. These reforms would not only contain violence but also signal that the region’s institutions are catching up with its aspirations for peace. Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger pzeiler Thu, 09/03/2026 - 16:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Podcast / Africa 03 September 2026 1 minutes Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger This week on The Horn , Alan talks with Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis, about the possible end of UNSOS, the UN logistics operation supporting African Union troops and Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab and what may come next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia In this episode of The Horn , Alan is joined by Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis about the U.S. decision to oppose renewed United Nations logistical support for the 19-year-old African Union military mission in Somalia. Samira explains why UN logistical support has been critical to the AU mission as well as to Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab, and why its loss could leave some areas outside Mogadishu increasingly vulnerable. They also discuss what could happen if no solution or stopgap measure is found, and the 12,000-strong African Union mission ceases to function by the end of the year. They discuss how such a scenario could shift the balance of power on the battlefield between the federal government and Al-Shabaab. They also assess whether Mogadishu’s pursuit of bilateral security partnerships could fill the void left by a weakened or defunct AU mission. This episode is produced in partnership with the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. Click here to listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . For more, check out Balqiis’ report “ No Time to Drift: Somalia and the Deadline for a Managed Security Transition ” and our Somalia page. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/04/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 04 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Friday 4 September HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. But countries that have this technology, including the U.S., the UK and Russia, oppose it, contending that current provisions under international humanitarian law are sufficient. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Beijing characterised the missile test as part of routine annual training that comports with international law, stressing that it was not directed at another country. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the test sends a signal to the U.S. and allies that Beijing is determined to push back against what it views as attempts to contain China’s rise. The test took place on the same day that Australia signed a mutual defence agreement with Fiji. It will likely push other Asia Pacific countries both to deepen such cooperation and to accelerate their own military modernisation. SOUTH SUDAN On Sunday, opposition fighters killed James Kueth Makuach, commissioner of Akobo county in Jonglei state, in what President Salva Kiir’s government described as an “assassination”. Makuach had belonged to the party of former Vice President Riek Machar, who was arrested on sedition charges last year amid fighting between his loyalists and government forces. In April, Makuach defected to Kiir’s camp. The president then reappointed him as county commissioner, breaching South Sudan’s 2018 peace accord, which allotted this post to Machar’s group. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the Akobo attack, which also took the lives of two other government officials, is part of an escalation in clashes in Jonglei over the past week. But it appears to have been an act of political retribution rather than a push for territory or another military objective. Makuach’s killing underscores the dangers of proceeding with national elections planned for December with no political consensus in Juba and swathes of the country embroiled in civil strife. 3 July 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. On Sunday, Pakistani forces once again carried out strikes across the border in Afghanistan, saying they killed 29 militants. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. The flare-up coincides with the arrival of the first Chadian troops under the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, as Kenyan officers who served in the Multinational Security Support mission begin to withdraw. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the attacks show that gangs remain entrenched despite having scaled back their activity in recent months. They control most of the capital Port-au-Prince and are likely assessing their next moves outside it. Haitian security forces must stand ready during the high-risk period ahead. Gangs could go on the offensive as the Kenya-led mission phases out and the new force takes over. IRAN In a speech Wednesday evening, President Donald Trump said the U.S. would hit Iran “extremely hard”, sending it “back to the Stone Age” by bombing power plants if Tehran does not acquiesce to U.S. terms for ending the war. He also claimed such a deal was nearing completion. Washington has meanwhile deployed thousands more troops in the region, while Iran has continued attacks on Israel and Gulf Arab neighbours. Tehran has also kept a stranglehold on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, as Yemen’s Houthis warn that further escalation could prompt them to close the Bab al-Mandab, increasing the strain on maritime traffic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says a month of U.S.-Israeli strikes have brought the Iranian regime no closer to capitulation. So long as Washington and Tehran are pressing maximalist demands, believing they can force the other to yield, the war risks getting worse. SYRIA Sectarian unrest erupted in the predominantly Christian town of Suqaylabiyah in western Syria last Saturday. An argument over allegations of harassment reportedly prompted hundreds of men from the neighbouring Sunni-majority town of Qalaat al-Madiq to rush into Suqaylabiyah, ransacking Christian shops, homes and other property. Clashes lasted for hours until government forces brought in reinforcements to restore order. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the episode underscores persistent shortcomings in Syria's security architecture. State forces tend to react to such incidents rather than help prevent them. Largely drawn from the Sunni majority, these forces lack understanding of minority groups, whose trust in the new authorities is fast eroding. Until the government addresses those weaknesses, the risk of more such violence will remain high – particularly in diverse areas where tensions built over fourteen years of war are still raw. 27 March 2026 IRAN With the Middle East war in its fourth week, the Trump administration submitted to Tehran, via Pakistani mediators, what U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff described as a “fifteen-point action list that forms the framework for a peace deal”. The plan, among other things, would reportedly require that the Islamic Republic give up its capacity to enrich uranium, which it has previously refused to do. Iran has countered with its own list of demands, including that the U.S. withdraw from all its military bases in the Gulf, which Washington has dismissed out of hand. Meanwhile, the U.S. is sending more ground troops to the region. A negotiated end to the conflict seems out of reach for now, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as each side thinks its wartime position remains favourable. More likely is a protracted standoff or, worse, a dramatic escalation. IRAQ Fresh hostilities erupted this week between the U.S. and Iraqi militias backed by Tehran. These groups belong to an umbrella institution, the Hashd al-Shaabi, that is formally under the aegis of the Iraqi military commander-in-chief, though some of them operate independently. Those aligned with Iran have launched several rockets at U.S. bases in Iraq and neighbouring countries. A retaliatory U.S. airstrike on the Hashd headquarters in Baghdad killed fifteen fighters and another on a military facility in western Iraq claimed seven more lives. Meanwhile, the peshmerga in Iraqi Kurdistan, who are friendly to Washington, said Iranian missiles hit one of their bases in Erbil, killing six. The Iraqi government protested the infringements upon its sovereignty. But it lacks the leverage to stop the deadly exchanges, says Crisis Group expert Lahib Higel. The country is also facing an impending fiscal crisis, as oil sales have declined steeply with the Strait of Hormuz mostly shut. SUDAN UN agencies issued statements Tuesday protesting a “sharp increase” in drone warfare that is taking a mounting civilian toll. At least 70 people were killed the previous day when drones hit a hospital in East Darfur. Patients, doctors and nurses were among the dead. Another 28 civilians were killed in drone strikes in North Darfur and North Kordofan Thursday. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says both main belligerents in Sudan’s war, the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), have stepped up their use of drones in an attempt to get an edge on the battlefield. Meanwhile, the risk of spillover into neighbouring countries is heightening, with the RSF taking a town on the Ethiopian border and fighting continuing on the Chadian frontier. 20 March 2026 CHAD - SUDAN A drone attack Wednesday killed seventeen people in Chad’s border town of Tine, including mourners gathered for a funeral and children playing nearby. The Chadian government accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan of launching the drone. In late February, the RSF had hit Chadian army positions in Tine, killing several Chadian soldiers. President Mahamat Déby ordered a total closure of the border with Sudan, which could have negative humanitarian consequences. The border has officially been closed since April 2023, but until now authorities have been allowing some refugees and aid shipments through. He also warned that Chad would retaliate for any further strikes on its territory, no matter who is responsible. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says Chad, which hosts around one million Sudanese refugees, increasingly risks getting drawn into the war in Sudan as fighting routinely spills across the border. IRAN Oil and gas prices soared and stock markets dived Thursday after Iran struck Qatar’s main natural gas facility, Ras Laffan. The Iranian attack came a day after Israel hit Iran’s South Pars gas field, one of the world’s largest. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these tit-for-tat attacks on hydrocarbon infrastructure signal a new phase in the conflict, now entering its fourth week, as a global energy crisis looms and Gulf Arab states are increasingly caught in the crossfire, with Saudi Arabia warning of military action against Iran as these states’ patience wears thin. NIGERIA Multiple suicide bombings Monday killed at least 26 people and injured over a hundred in Maiduguri, capital of Nigeria’s Borno state. The attacks mark the second deadliest incident in Maiduguri in the past five years. No group has yet claimed responsibility. The bombings come amid a surge of violence in the country’s north east, with both Boko Haram and the Islamic State-West Africa Province, an ISIS affiliate, launching lethal raids. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest attacks indicate that these insurgencies may again be gaining momentum. The Nigerian government and its foreign partners should step up efforts to counter the new challenge and halt rising insecurity in other parts of the country. 13 March 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Drone strikes killed several people Tuesday night in Goma, capital of North Kivu province in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including a French woman working with UNICEF and at least two other residents. The M23 rebels who hold the city blamed the Congolese government for the attacks. Kinshasa said an investigation is under way. Despite a formal ceasefire in their conflict, both the Congolese government and the M23 (backed by Rwandan troops) have been acquiring drones as a means of getting around enemy defences. Tuesday’s attacks, along with another in February that killed M23 spokesperson Willy Ngoma, mark a dramatic escalation in the conflict’s aerial warfare. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says Kinshasa, which has purchased Chinese and Turkish drones, is determined to use its new arsenal to show the rebels they are not safe in their bastions. But with civilian casualties mounting, the government’s growing reliance on drones could backfire by costing it international support. Having flexed its muscles, Kinshasa would be well advised to return to the diplomatic arena, pressing for Rwandan withdrawal from the country and returning to negotiations with the M23 with a stronger hand. IRAN Amid a widening Middle East conflict sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes that began two weeks ago, the Islamic Republic effected only the second transition in its most senior post since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. Mojtaba Khamenei has taken up the position of Supreme Leader, which his father Ali held from 1989 until his death on 28 February in the war’s opening salvo. The U.S.-Israeli campaign has continued unabated, doing significant damage. Iran has responded with drone and missile strikes in the Gulf and brought traffic in the Strait of Hormuz to a crawl. The first official statement attributed to the younger Khamenei was defiant in tone, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, highlighting the Iranian regime's desire to project continuity under duress, vis-à-vis both its foreign adversaries and its domestic opponents. But that ambition could be short-lived if Khamenei is targeted amid the hostilities or outmanoeuvred by other players in the regime's upper echelons. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. Since 2 March, when Hizbollah fired rockets toward Israeli territory for the first time in over a year, Israel has ramped up aerial bombardment, including of the capital Beirut, and forced hundreds of thousands to flee their homes. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. Suweida’s Exam Standoff Triggers Fresh Clashes in Southern Syria pzeiler Fri, 09/04/2026 - 14:57 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Middle East & North Africa 04 September 2026 2 minutes Suweida’s Exam Standoff Triggers Fresh Clashes in Southern Syria Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach analyses a week of tensions in the Syrian province as government forces and local Druze troops once again trade fire Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Nanar Hawach Senior Analyst, Syria Related Tags Syria Tensions soared in late August between the Syrian government in Damascus and local forces in Suweida , a Druze-majority southern province that has stood outside government control since fighting in July 2025 killed over 1,700 . The immediate trigger for the unrest came on 19 August, when Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa decreed that some 13,000 students in Suweida should sit school exams in government-held parts of the province north of Suweida city, rather than in the city itself. Students had missed the regular exams in June due to the prolonged standoff between Damascus and the de facto local administration led by Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, a Druze spiritual leader. His so-called “National Guard” troops control much of the province, having benefitted from Israeli strikes against Syrian government forces during the July 2025 turmoil. On 24 August, al-Hijri doubled down, stating that the Druze are “an integral part of Israel” and share with it “even in creed”, claiming religious kinship – comments that drew widespread criticism within Druze communities. His remarks were also the latest instance of al-Hijri implying Israeli support for a separatist agenda, which Tel Aviv has thus far refrained from endorsing. Two days later, the “Shahba Operations Room”, an armed group allied to the National Guard, announced road closures and objected to exams being held in villages it considers “occupied”. On 29 August, thousands of students nevertheless boarded buses organised under local initiatives in a bid to get to the exam centres, before forces allied with the National Guard attacked the vehicles and obliged them to turn back. Reportedly, no students travelling from Suweida made it to the exams. Clashes broke out that night as the National Guard and Syrian forces exchanged mortar and heavy machine-gun fire, allegedly killing two civilians and a fighter in the Guard. Each side accused the other of firing first, but neither side gained any ground and calm finally returned on 1 September. These latest troubles illustrate the risk that Suweida’s conflict, while seemingly frozen, could flare up at the slightest provocation. Damascus and Suweida are locked in a struggle over who controls the workings of the state and public services. For Damascus, holding exams in areas under its control is an exercise of central state authority; for Suweida ’s Druze leadership, it is a challenge to their aspirations for autonomy. The costs of this struggle are increasingly falling on Suweida’s residents: without access to resources and state services, public frustrations within the province are likely to grow. The episode should serve as a warning to all involved over the huge potential costs of any resumption of conflict. Damascus should take care to avoid further military build-up in the areas and continue to work with contacts in Suweida on pragmatic solutions to the problems thrown up by the standoff. While Damascus’s control over state resources has increased pressure on al-Hijri’s camp, applying them to rebuild trust with Suweida’s residents could ultimately prove a wiser course of action.
